title: Reactions, Energy and the Nucleus
bigQuestion: What really changes in a chemical or nuclear reaction, and what stays exactly the same?

story.title: The Pile Under the Stadium
story.kicker: On a cold December afternoon in 1942, a stack of graphite bricks on a Chicago squash court did something no human had ever made matter do.
paragraphs: Stagg Field was the University of Chicago's football stadium, and by 1942 the team was gone. Under the west stands was an abandoned squash court, unheated, with a high ceiling. In it, a team led by the Italian physicist Enrico Fermi had spent weeks stacking bricks of graphite, a pure form of carbon, into a rough black sphere. Inside the pile, at careful intervals, sat lumps of uranium. They called the thing Chicago Pile-1.

The idea came from a discovery made in Germany four years earlier. When a slow neutron strikes a uranium nucleus, the nucleus can split into two smaller pieces and release energy, along with two or three fresh neutrons. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch worked out what was happening and named it fission. Physicists saw the next step at once. If each fission released neutrons that caused more fissions, the reaction could feed itself. A chain reaction.

Nobody knew for certain that it would work. Neutrons leak out, get absorbed, or fly too fast to be caught. The graphite was there to slow them down. Cadmium rods, which soak up neutrons, were pushed into the pile to hold the reaction back. On December 2, the rods came out a few inches at a time while instruments clicked and a pen traced the neutron count on a rolling chart. Each time, the count rose and leveled off. Fermi did his arithmetic on a slide rule.

At about 3:25 in the afternoon he ordered the last rod pulled out another foot. The clicking became a roar, and the pen line on the chart stopped leveling off. It climbed in a straight line. The pile was making its own neutrons faster than it lost them. Fermi let it run for several minutes, then had the rods driven back in. The power had been tiny, less than a light bulb. But the reaction had sustained itself.

A physicist named Arthur Compton phoned a colleague in Washington with a coded message: the Italian navigator had landed in the New World. Someone opened a bottle of Chianti and the roughly fifty people present drank from paper cups. Within three years the same physics produced two bombs and, a decade later, the first power plants. This chapter is about what changes in every reaction, chemical or nuclear, and the one thing that never does.
story.think: The team could not see a single neutron. What evidence convinced them that the reaction had become self-sustaining, and why was that evidence trustworthy?

lessons.title: Atoms Are Rearranged, Not Destroyed
lessons.mainIdea: In a chemical reaction, atoms break old bonds and form new ones, but no atom is created or destroyed, so mass is conserved.
reading: Burn a log in a fireplace and by morning only a handful of ash remains. It looks as though most of the wood simply disappeared. In the 1770s the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier began weighing everything, including the gases, in sealed glass vessels before and after a reaction. He found that the total mass never changed. The wood had not vanished; it had become carbon dioxide and water vapor that drifted up the chimney.

This is the *law of conservation of mass*: in a chemical reaction, the total mass of the starting materials equals the total mass of the products. The reason is simple once you know about atoms. A reaction only rearranges them. Bonds between atoms break, and new bonds form, but every carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atom that went in comes out somewhere. Atoms are like letters; a reaction spells new words with the same letters.

Chemists write this rearrangement as a *chemical equation*. The *reactants*, the starting materials, go on the left. An arrow means reacts to form. The *products* go on the right. Burning methane, the main part of natural gas, is written CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O. One carbon, four hydrogens and four oxygens on the left; one carbon, four hydrogens and four oxygens on the right. Nothing lost.

Conservation of mass lets you do real accounting. If 16 grams of methane burn completely, they use 64 grams of oxygen and make exactly 80 grams of carbon dioxide and water combined. A car's exhaust weighs more than the gasoline it burned because it includes the oxygen pulled from the air. The mass does not appear from nowhere; it was in the air all along.

words.d: the rule that the total mass of the products of a chemical reaction equals the total mass of the reactants
a way of writing a reaction with symbols: reactants on the left, an arrow, products on the right
a substance that goes into a chemical reaction and is changed by it
a substance that is made by a chemical reaction

look.title: Lavoisier's Rule
look.text: In his 1789 textbook Lavoisier stated the principle in effect this way: nothing is created in the operations of art or of nature, and it can be taken as a law that in every process there is the same quantity of matter before and after; the elements are only changed in their combinations.
look.cite: Antoine Lavoisier, Elementary Treatise on Chemistry, 1789
look.prompt: Lavoisier could not see atoms. What kind of measurements would let him state this rule with confidence anyway?

check.q: A candle burns and loses mass. Where did the missing mass go?
choices: It was destroyed by the flame
It turned into heat and light
It became gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapor that spread into the air
check.why: Atoms are not destroyed. The wax's carbon and hydrogen combined with oxygen to form gases that left the candle.

check.q: In the equation CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O, which substances are the reactants?
check.why: Reactants are on the left of the arrow: methane and oxygen.

check.q: If 4 grams of hydrogen react completely with 32 grams of oxygen, what mass of water forms?
check.why: Mass is conserved: 4 + 32 = 36 grams of product.

lessons.title: Balancing an Equation
lessons.mainIdea: Balancing an equation means adjusting the numbers in front of formulas until every element has the same count on both sides.
reading: Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen to make water. A first attempt at the equation, H2 + O2 → H2O, has a problem. Two oxygen atoms go in but only one comes out. That would violate conservation of mass. You cannot fix it by changing H2O to H2O2, because that is a different substance, hydrogen peroxide. The formulas are fixed by nature. Only the amounts can change.

The fix is a *coefficient*, a whole number in front of a formula that counts molecules. Write 2 H2O and now there are two oxygens on the right. But there are also four hydrogens on the right and only two on the left, so put a 2 in front of H2 as well. The *balanced equation* is 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. Count it: four hydrogens and two oxygens on each side.

A reliable method: list each element and count it on both sides. Balance the element that appears in the fewest formulas first. Save hydrogen and oxygen for last, since they often show up in several places. Never touch a subscript. Adjust one coefficient, recount, and repeat until the columns match. Rust forming on an iron nail, 4 Fe + 3 O2 → 2 Fe2O3, takes two or three rounds.

The coefficients are more than bookkeeping. They give the ratio in which the substances react. Two molecules of hydrogen for every one of oxygen, or two truckloads for every one, the ratio holds. A rocket engineer sizing fuel tanks and a baker adjusting a recipe are doing the same arithmetic on different scales. The balanced equation is the recipe card.

words.d: the whole number in front of a formula in an equation that tells how many of that molecule or unit take part
a chemical equation in which each element has the same number of atoms on both sides
the fixed proportion in which substances react, given by the coefficients

look.title: The Nail in the Jar
look.text: An iron nail is sealed in a jar with air and weighed. After two weeks it is orange with rust. The sealed jar weighs exactly the same as before. Then the jar is opened and the nail alone is weighed. It is heavier than it was when clean.
look.prompt: Why did the sealed jar keep the same mass while the nail gained mass? Write the rust equation and use it in your answer.

check.q: Which change is allowed when balancing an equation?
choices: Changing a subscript inside a formula
Changing a coefficient in front of a formula
check.why: Coefficients change how many of each molecule react; subscripts define the substance and cannot be altered.

check.q: What coefficient balances the equation N2 + ? H2 → 2 NH3?
check.why: Two NH3 contain six hydrogens, so three H2 molecules are needed.

check.q: In 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O, how many oxygen atoms are on each side?
choices: 2 on the left and 1 on the right
check.why: One O2 has two oxygen atoms; two H2O molecules together also have two.

lessons.title: Five Kinds of Reactions
lessons.mainIdea: Most reactions fit a few patterns: synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement and combustion.
reading: Chemists have sorted reactions into a few families by the shape of the change. In *synthesis*, two or more substances join to make one: 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O, or iron and sulfur heated together to make iron sulfide. In *decomposition*, one substance breaks into two or more: an electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, and heat breaks calcium carbonate, limestone, into lime and carbon dioxide.

In a *single replacement* reaction, one element trades places with another in a compound. Drop a zinc strip into blue copper sulfate solution and the zinc dissolves while reddish copper metal appears: Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu. A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out. This is how the reactivity trends from the periodic table show up in a beaker.

In a *double replacement* reaction, two compounds swap partners. Mix clear solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride and a white solid, silver chloride, appears instantly and sinks. The solid that forms from two solutions is called a precipitate. Water treatment plants, including those along Lake Michigan, use this kind of reaction to pull unwanted ions out of drinking water.

*Combustion* is a reaction with oxygen that releases heat and light. A fuel made of carbon and hydrogen burns to carbon dioxide and water. Fires, engines and furnaces all run on combustion. It is also the reaction that has changed the atmosphere most since the 1800s. Knowing the family of a reaction lets you predict its products before you run it, which is a large part of what chemistry is for.

words.d: a reaction in which two or more substances combine to form one
a reaction in which one substance breaks apart into two or more
a reaction in which one element takes the place of another in a compound
a reaction in which two compounds exchange partners
a reaction with oxygen that releases heat and light; burning

look.title: Zinc in the Blue Solution
look.text: A student places a strip of zinc in a beaker of blue copper sulfate solution. Over ten minutes the blue fades, the zinc strip grows thinner, and a reddish-brown crust forms on it. She then places a strip of copper in a colorless zinc sulfate solution and waits. Nothing happens.
look.prompt: Classify the first reaction, and explain using reactivity why the second one does nothing.

check.q: Heating limestone (CaCO3) produces lime (CaO) and carbon dioxide. What type of reaction is this?
check.why: One substance breaks into two: a decomposition.

check.q: Two clear solutions are mixed and a white solid forms. What has most likely happened?
choices: A double replacement reaction produced an insoluble compound
check.why: Two compounds swapped partners, and one new pairing does not dissolve, so it appears as a precipitate.

check.q: Why does zinc replace copper in copper sulfate, but copper does not replace zinc in zinc sulfate?
choices: Zinc is the more reactive metal and gives up its electrons more easily
Zinc dissolves in water on its own
check.why: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of a compound; the reverse does not happen.

lessons.title: Collisions and Reaction Rate
lessons.mainIdea: Reactions happen when particles collide hard enough and in the right way, so anything that makes effective collisions more frequent speeds up a reaction.
reading: A steel ship rusts over decades. Steel wool held in a flame burns in seconds. Both are iron reacting with oxygen. Why does one take a lifetime and the other a moment? The *reaction rate* depends on how often particles hit each other with enough energy to break bonds. Chemists call this collision theory. No collision, no reaction. Weak collision, no reaction either.

Every reaction has an energy hill to climb before it can go downhill. The height of the hill is the *activation energy*. Wood does not burst into flame on the shelf because room-temperature collisions rarely have enough energy to get over the hill. Touch a match to it and the local temperature rises, collisions get harder, and enough of them make it over that the reaction can heat the next bit of wood itself.

Four factors change the rate. *Temperature*: hotter particles move faster and collide harder and more often. *Concentration*: more particles in the same space means more collisions; a fire in pure oxygen is far fiercer than in air. *Surface area*: only the outside of a solid can react, so powder burns faster than a lump. Flour dust in a grain elevator can explode, which is why Illinois elevators control dust so carefully. Sawdust is dangerous where a plank is not.

The fourth factor is a *catalyst*, a substance that lowers the activation energy without being used up. It gives the particles an easier path over the hill. A car's catalytic converter uses platinum to speed the conversion of exhaust gases. Every living cell runs on catalysts called enzymes, which let reactions that would take years happen in a fraction of a second at body temperature.

words.d: how fast reactants change into products
the minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to happen
how much of a substance is packed into a given volume
a substance that speeds a reaction by lowering its activation energy and is not used up

look.title: The Sugar Cube and the Sugar Dust
look.text: A sugar cube held in a flame with tongs blackens slowly at the edges and barely burns. A pinch of powdered sugar blown across the same flame flashes into a bright fireball. Same sugar, same flame, same amount of oxygen in the room.
look.prompt: Use collision theory to explain the difference. Which of the four rate factors is doing the work here?

check.q: Why does raising the temperature usually speed up a reaction?
choices: Particles move faster, so they collide more often and with more energy
check.why: Hotter particles collide harder and more frequently, so more collisions clear the energy hill.

check.q: What does a catalyst do?
choices: Gets used up to make more product
Lowers the activation energy without being consumed
Raises the temperature of the reactants
check.why: A catalyst provides an easier pathway and comes out unchanged at the end.

check.q: A lump of coal burns slowly, but coal dust can explode. Which factor explains this?
choices: Activation energy is lower for dust
check.why: Dust exposes far more surface to oxygen, so many more collisions happen at once.

lessons.title: Energy Stored in Bonds
lessons.mainIdea: Breaking bonds takes energy and forming bonds releases it; a reaction is exothermic if it releases more than it absorbs, endothermic if it absorbs more.
reading: Crack open a chemical hand warmer and it grows hot in your pocket for hours. Squeeze an instant cold pack and it turns icy against a sprained ankle. In one, a reaction gives off energy; in the other, a process soaks it up. Both come down to the same accounting: it costs energy to break a bond, and forming a bond pays energy back. The difference between the cost and the payback is the energy you feel.

A reaction that releases more energy than it absorbs is *exothermic*. Burning methane breaks the C–H and O=O bonds, which costs energy, then forms C=O and O–H bonds, which returns more. The surplus leaves as heat and light. The products hold less stored energy than the reactants did. Rusting, combustion, and the reaction of sodium with water are all exothermic. Hand warmers use iron rusting fast.

A reaction that absorbs more energy than it releases is *endothermic*. Baking soda mixed with vinegar makes the cup feel cool. Photosynthesis is the largest endothermic reaction on Earth: a leaf uses sunlight to push carbon dioxide and water uphill into sugar and oxygen. The energy does not vanish. It is stored in the new bonds and comes back out when you burn the wood or digest the sugar.

Chemists draw this as an energy diagram. Reactants sit at one height, products at another, with the activation energy hill between them. An exothermic reaction ends lower than it started; an endothermic one ends higher. Energy, like mass, is conserved. What a reaction gives off, it took from its bonds; what it absorbs, it stores. The total in the universe is unchanged.

words.d: describes a reaction that releases more energy than it absorbs, usually as heat
describes a reaction that absorbs more energy than it releases, so its surroundings cool
the energy needed to break a particular bond, or released when that bond forms

look.title: Energy to Break One Mole of Bonds
look.prompt: Nitrogen gas, N2, makes up most of the air yet barely reacts. Use the table to explain why.

check.q: Which statement about bonds and energy is correct?
choices: Both breaking and forming release energy
Breaking bonds requires energy; forming bonds releases it
check.why: It costs energy to pull bonded atoms apart and energy is paid back when new bonds form.

check.q: A reaction in a beaker makes the beaker feel cold. The reaction is:
choices: Endothermic, absorbing energy from its surroundings
check.why: The reaction takes heat from the beaker and your hand, so it is endothermic.

check.q: In an exothermic reaction, how does the stored energy of the products compare to the reactants?
check.why: The surplus energy left as heat, so the products hold less than the reactants did.

lessons.title: Equilibrium: Reactions That Run Both Ways
lessons.mainIdea: Many reactions can run forward and backward; at equilibrium both directions happen at the same rate, and changing conditions shifts the balance.
reading: Open a bottle of soda and it fizzes. Inside the sealed bottle, carbon dioxide gas was dissolving into the liquid at exactly the same rate that dissolved gas was escaping back out. Nothing looked like it was happening, but two opposite processes were running at full speed and canceling. This balance is *equilibrium*. Open the cap, the pressure drops, and the balance tips toward escape.

Many chemical reactions are *reversible*. The products can react to re-form the reactants. When the forward and reverse rates become equal, the amounts stop changing, though individual molecules keep switching back and forth. It is like a crowded room with one door: people go in and out constantly, but the number inside holds steady.

Push on an equilibrium and it pushes back. Add more of a reactant and the forward reaction speeds up until a new balance forms with more product. Remove a product as it forms and the reaction keeps making more to replace it. Raise the temperature and the balance shifts toward the direction that absorbs heat. Chemists use this to steer reactions toward the product they want.

The most important example feeds the world. Nitrogen and hydrogen combine to make ammonia, the base of most fertilizer, but the reaction is reversible and slow. In the early 1900s Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch found that high pressure, moderate heat and an iron catalyst push the balance toward ammonia and make it fast enough to be practical. Much of the nitrogen in the corn and soybeans grown across Illinois arrives through this one equilibrium.

words.d: the state in which a forward reaction and its reverse happen at the same rate, so amounts stop changing
describes a reaction whose products can change back into the reactants
a change in the balance of an equilibrium toward more products or more reactants after conditions change

look.title: The Crowded Room
look.text: Picture a party room with one door. Every minute, ten people walk in and ten walk out. The crowd inside stays at 100. Now the host puts out free pizza. For a while more people come in than leave, until the room holds 150 and the flow in and out is equal again.
look.prompt: Match each part of the story to an idea from the lesson: forward rate, reverse rate, equilibrium, and a shift. What is the pizza?

check.q: At equilibrium, which is true?
choices: Only the forward reaction is happening
The forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate
check.why: Both directions continue, but at equal rates, so the amounts stay steady.

check.q: A reversible reaction is at equilibrium. More reactant is added. What happens?
choices: The balance shifts to make more product
check.why: Extra reactant speeds the forward direction until a new balance with more product is reached.

check.q: Why is the ammonia process run at high pressure?
choices: Pressure is needed to melt the iron catalyst
High pressure pushes the balance toward ammonia and speeds the reaction
check.why: Pressure favors the side with fewer gas molecules, which is ammonia, and helps the reaction go fast enough to be useful.

lessons.title: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life
lessons.mainIdea: An unstable nucleus changes by emitting radiation, and each radioactive isotope has a fixed half-life, the time for half its atoms to decay.
reading: In 1896 the French physicist Henri Becquerel left a uranium salt on a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer. When he developed the plate, it was fogged as if by light. The uranium was giving off something invisible on its own, with no sunlight and no reaction. Marie and Pierre Curie tracked the effect, found two new elements that did it far more strongly, and named the phenomenon *radioactivity*.

Chemical reactions never touch the nucleus. Radioactive decay is a change in the nucleus itself. An unstable nucleus throws out a piece and becomes a different, more stable nucleus. *Alpha* decay ejects a bundle of two protons and two neutrons; the atom drops two places on the periodic table. *Beta* decay turns a neutron into a proton and shoots out an electron; the atom moves up one place. *Gamma* rays are pure energy, released as the nucleus settles.

You cannot predict when one particular nucleus will decay. But a large group decays at a perfectly steady rate, and that rate is described by the *half-life*: the time for half the atoms in a sample to decay. After one half-life, half remain. After two, a quarter. After three, an eighth. The half-life is a fixed property of the isotope. Heat, pressure and chemical bonding do not change it at all.

Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years. Iodine-131, used in treating thyroid disease, has a half-life of about 8 days, so it is gone from a patient within weeks. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, close to the age of Earth, so about half of the original uranium in the planet is still here. Long half-lives make radioactive waste a long-term problem; short ones make some isotopes safe to use in medicine.

words.d: the process by which an unstable nucleus gives off particles or energy and changes into a different nucleus
the time it takes for half the atoms of a radioactive isotope in a sample to decay
two protons and two neutrons ejected together from a nucleus during alpha decay
an electron ejected from a nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton

look.title: Half-Lives of Some Isotopes
look.prompt: A hospital wants an isotope for a body scan that will be almost gone in two days. Which one on the list fits, and why would a long-lived isotope be a bad choice?

check.q: A sample holds 800 atoms of an isotope with a half-life of 10 years. How many remain after 30 years?
check.why: Three half-lives: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100.

check.q: Which of these changes the half-life of an isotope?
choices: None of these; half-life is fixed
check.why: Half-life is a property of the nucleus and is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.

check.q: How does radioactive decay differ from a chemical reaction?
choices: Decay changes the nucleus and can turn one element into another; chemical reactions only rearrange electrons and bonds
check.why: Chemistry leaves the nucleus untouched, so the element never changes; decay alters the nucleus itself.

lessons.title: Carbon Dating
lessons.mainIdea: Living things constantly take in carbon-14; after death it decays with a 5,730-year half-life, so the amount left tells how long ago the organism died.
reading: High in the atmosphere, cosmic rays strike nitrogen atoms and turn a few of them into carbon-14. That radioactive carbon mixes into carbon dioxide, and plants breathe it in during photosynthesis. Animals eat the plants. So every living thing carries a small, steady trace of carbon-14, about one atom in a trillion, replaced as fast as it decays. The moment the organism dies, the intake stops and the clock starts.

Carbon-14 decays by beta emission back into nitrogen with a half-life of about 5,730 years. A piece of wood that has half the carbon-14 of a living tree died about 5,730 years ago. A quarter means about 11,460 years. By counting the decays in a sample, or by counting the atoms directly, a lab can date bone, wood, cloth, charcoal or seeds. This is *radiocarbon dating*.

The method was worked out by the chemist Willard Libby at the University of Chicago in the late 1940s, and it earned him the Nobel Prize in 1960. He tested it on wood from Egyptian tombs whose ages were already known from written records, and the dates matched. That check against independent evidence is what turned a clever idea into a trusted tool. Archaeologists use it to date the burned corn and charcoal of the ancient mound-builders at Cahokia, near Collinsville, Illinois.

The method has limits, and honest scientists state them. After about ten half-lives, roughly 50,000 years, too little carbon-14 remains to measure, so dinosaur bones cannot be carbon dated. The amount of carbon-14 in the air has varied a little over time, so raw dates are corrected using tree rings of known age. Other isotopes with longer half-lives, such as uranium and potassium, date rocks that are millions or billions of years old.

words.d: a method of finding the age of once-living material by measuring how much carbon-14 remains
a high-energy particle from space that can change atoms in the upper atmosphere
correcting a measurement against samples of known value, such as tree rings of known age

look.title: Two Charcoal Samples
look.text: A lab receives two pieces of charcoal from a dig. Sample A contains about one-half the carbon-14 of fresh wood. Sample B contains about one-eighth. The dig director also notes that Sample B came from a deeper layer than Sample A.
look.prompt: Estimate the age of each sample. Does the layering agree with the dates? What would you conclude if it did not?

check.q: Why does a living tree keep a steady level of carbon-14?
choices: It takes in new carbon-14 from the air as fast as the old decays
Carbon-14 does not decay in living tissue
Sunlight makes carbon-14 in the leaves
check.why: Photosynthesis keeps supplying fresh carbon-14, replacing what decays.

check.q: A bone has one-quarter the carbon-14 of a living animal. About how old is it?
check.why: One-quarter means two half-lives have passed: 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years.

check.q: Why can't carbon dating be used on a 70-million-year-old dinosaur fossil?
choices: After so many half-lives, no measurable carbon-14 is left
Fossils are too heavy to test
Carbon-14 was not present in the air back then
check.why: After roughly 50,000 years, too little carbon-14 remains to count. Other isotopes date such old material.

lessons.title: Fission and Fusion
lessons.mainIdea: Splitting a heavy nucleus or joining light ones releases enormous energy because a small amount of mass turns into energy.
reading: Burning a kilogram of coal releases enough energy to boil a bathtub or two of water. Splitting a kilogram of uranium releases millions of times more. The difference is that chemical reactions only rearrange electrons, while nuclear reactions rearrange the nucleus, where the forces are vastly stronger. In a nuclear change, a tiny fraction of the mass disappears, and it reappears as energy according to Einstein's equation E = mc².

*Fission* is the splitting of a heavy nucleus. When a neutron is absorbed by uranium-235, the nucleus wobbles and breaks into two smaller nuclei, such as barium and krypton, and releases two or three more neutrons plus a burst of energy. If those neutrons hit other uranium-235 nuclei, the process repeats and grows. This is the *chain reaction* that Fermi's pile achieved under Stagg Field.

*Fusion* is the opposite: joining light nuclei into a heavier one. In the core of the sun, at about 15 million degrees Celsius, hydrogen nuclei are slammed together so hard that they fuse into helium. The helium weighs slightly less than the hydrogen that made it, and that missing mass is the sunlight that reaches Illinois eight minutes later. Fusion powers every star and releases even more energy per kilogram than fission.

Fission is used in every nuclear power plant today because it can be started and controlled at ordinary temperatures. Fusion needs star-like heat and pressure to force the positive nuclei past their repulsion. Laboratories have produced brief bursts of fusion energy, and research reactors are being built, but no fusion plant yet delivers electricity to a grid. Its fuel is plentiful and its waste is far less long-lived, which is why the effort continues.

words.d: the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing neutrons and energy
the joining of light nuclei into a heavier one, releasing energy, as in the sun
a reaction in which the neutrons from one fission trigger more fissions, so the process keeps itself going

look.title: Fermi Describes the Pile
look.text: Writing after the war, Fermi explained the plan in plain terms. Fissioning uranium releases more than one neutron on average. If enough of those neutrons could be made to cause further fissions instead of escaping or being absorbed, the reaction would sustain itself. Graphite was chosen to slow the neutrons, because slow neutrons are captured by uranium-235 far more readily than fast ones.
look.cite: Enrico Fermi, account of the first chain-reacting pile, 1946
look.prompt: Why did the team need to slow the neutrons down rather than speed them up? What does that tell you about how fission depends on collisions?

check.q: Why do nuclear reactions release so much more energy than chemical reactions?
choices: They change the nucleus, and a small amount of mass is converted to energy
check.why: Nuclear forces are far stronger than chemical bonds, and the lost mass becomes energy by E = mc².

check.q: What makes a fission chain reaction possible?
choices: Each fission releases neutrons that can cause more fissions
Fission absorbs neutrons from the air
check.why: The extra neutrons from each split trigger further splits, so the reaction feeds itself.

check.q: Which statement about fusion is correct?
choices: It splits heavy nuclei like uranium
It runs all of today's power plants
It joins light nuclei and powers the sun
It requires no heat to start
check.why: Fusion joins light nuclei such as hydrogen into helium at enormous temperatures; it is what the sun does.

lessons.title: How a Reactor Works
lessons.mainIdea: A nuclear power plant uses a controlled fission chain reaction to make heat, which boils water to spin a turbine, just as a coal plant does with fire.
reading: Chicago Pile-1 produced less power than a flashlight. A modern reactor produces enough electricity for a city, but the idea is the same. Uranium fuel, enriched so that it holds a few percent uranium-235, is sealed in metal rods. Water flows around the rods. It serves two jobs at once: it slows the neutrons, as Fermi's graphite did, and it carries away the heat. A large reactor is mostly plumbing.

Control rods made of neutron-absorbing materials such as boron or cadmium slide in and out among the fuel. Pushed in, they soak up neutrons and the chain reaction slows. Pulled out, more neutrons survive to cause fission and the power rises. Operators keep the reaction exactly balanced, so that each fission leads on average to exactly one more. Push the rods fully in and the reaction stops within seconds.

The heat boils water into steam, either directly or through a second loop of pipes. The steam spins a *turbine*, which spins a generator that makes electricity. From the turbine onward, a nuclear plant is identical to a coal or gas plant. The difference is the source of heat: a nuclear reactor burns nothing, so it releases no carbon dioxide or smoke while running.

Illinois has more nuclear reactors than any other state, and they supply roughly half of the electricity generated here. One of the first commercial nuclear plants in the country opened in 1960 at Dresden, near Morris, about 60 miles southwest of Chicago. The concrete domes visible from the interstate house reactors that trace directly back to the pile under Stagg Field.

words.d: a rod of neutron-absorbing material that operators move to slow or speed a reactor's chain reaction
uranium processed to contain a higher share of uranium-235 than natural uranium has
a set of blades spun by steam or water to turn a generator
a material such as water or graphite that slows neutrons so they are more easily captured by uranium-235

look.title: The Rods Come Out
look.text: In the control room, an operator slowly withdraws the control rods. The neutron counter climbs and steadies. She withdraws them a little more; it climbs and steadies again. Then, at one setting, the counter begins rising steadily and does not level off. She immediately inserts the rods, and the count falls.
look.prompt: Explain what each stage of the counter's behavior tells the operator about the balance of neutrons in the core.

check.q: What is the purpose of a control rod?
choices: To carry heat to the turbine
To absorb neutrons and regulate the chain reaction
check.why: Control rods soak up neutrons; moving them in or out slows or speeds the reaction.

check.q: How does a nuclear plant turn fission into electricity?
choices: Heat from fission boils water, and the steam spins a turbine and generator
Uranium is burned in a furnace
check.why: Fission provides the heat; from the steam onward the plant works like any steam power plant.

check.q: Why is the water in a reactor doing two jobs?
choices: It cools the fuel and also slows neutrons so they are captured more easily
It dissolves the uranium and cleans the rods
It produces the neutrons and the electricity
It stops the reaction and stores the waste
check.why: Water carries away heat and acts as a moderator, slowing neutrons like Fermi's graphite did.

lessons.title: Benefits, Risks and Trade-offs
lessons.mainIdea: Nuclear power provides steady, low-carbon electricity, but it produces long-lived waste and carries rare but serious accident risks; weighing these is a decision about evidence and values.
reading: Every energy source is a trade. The evidence on nuclear power's benefits is clear. A reactor runs day and night regardless of wind or weather, and it emits no carbon dioxide while operating. A single fuel pellet the size of a fingertip yields about as much energy as a ton of coal. Measured per unit of electricity, the deaths caused by nuclear power over its history are far fewer than those from coal, which kills through air pollution and mining every year.

The risks are also real. Spent fuel stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years, and the United States still has no permanent underground storage site; waste sits in pools and steel casks at the plants, including those in Illinois. Accidents are rare but severe. The 1986 explosion at Chernobyl in the Soviet Union spread radioactive material across Europe. The 2011 earthquake and tsunami at Fukushima in Japan caused three reactor cores to melt and forced the evacuation of more than a hundred thousand people.

Cost is a third factor. Nuclear plants are expensive and slow to build, often taking a decade, while the fuel itself is cheap. Wind and solar have become cheaper to build but produce nothing on a still night. Natural gas is cheap and flexible but releases carbon dioxide. Engineers compare these using the same tools you would: cost, benefit, and the constraints of place, time and safety.

Reasonable people looking at the same evidence reach different conclusions, because they weigh a certain, ongoing harm against a rare, catastrophic one differently. A good argument in this debate states the evidence, acknowledges what it does not settle, and says which values tip the decision. That is not a weakness of science; it is where science hands the question to citizens.

words.d: used reactor fuel that is no longer efficient for fission but remains highly radioactive
a choice in which gaining one benefit means accepting a cost or giving up another
an accident in which reactor fuel overheats and melts because cooling has failed
producing little or no carbon dioxide while generating energy

look.title: The Letter to the President
look.text: In August 1939, a letter signed by Albert Einstein warned President Roosevelt that recent work suggested uranium could be made into a new and important source of energy in the near future, and that this might also lead to extremely powerful bombs. It urged the government to stay in touch with the physicists working on chain reactions.
look.cite: Albert Einstein and Leo Szilard, letter to Franklin D. Roosevelt, August 2, 1939
look.prompt: The same physics appears here as both an energy source and a weapon. How should that shape the way societies decide about nuclear technology?

check.q: Which is a well-supported benefit of nuclear power?
choices: It produces no waste of any kind
It releases no carbon dioxide while generating electricity
Its plants are quick and cheap to build
check.why: Reactors burn nothing, so they emit no carbon dioxide in operation; the other claims are false.

check.q: Why is spent nuclear fuel a long-term problem?
choices: It is too heavy to move
It remains radioactive for thousands of years and there is no permanent storage site in the U.S.
check.why: Long half-lives keep the waste hazardous for millennia, and permanent disposal has not been settled.

check.q: Two students read the same evidence about nuclear power and reach opposite conclusions. What is the most likely reason?
choices: One of them misread the data
They weigh a steady, certain harm against a rare, severe one differently
Science has no evidence on this question
Nuclear power has no benefits or risks
check.why: The evidence is shared; the difference is in how each person values different kinds of risk.

review.q: What did Chicago Pile-1 demonstrate on December 2, 1942?
choices: That uranium could be split for the first time
That a fission chain reaction could sustain itself
review.why: Fission had been discovered in 1938; the pile showed that fissions could keep triggering more fissions on their own.
Four hydrogens and two oxygens appear on each side only in the second choice.

review.q: A reaction gives off heat. Compared to the reactants, the products:
review.why: Exothermic reactions release stored bond energy, leaving products at lower energy. Mass and atom count stay the same.

review.q: Which change would slow a reaction down?
choices: Grinding the solid reactant into powder
review.why: Colder particles collide less often and less energetically; the other three all speed the reaction.

review.q: A reversible reaction at equilibrium has a product removed as it forms. The system will:
review.why: Removing product tips the balance forward, so more product is made to replace it.

review.q: An isotope has a half-life of 5 years. What fraction of a sample remains after 15 years?
Which statement correctly contrasts fission and fusion?
choices: Fission joins light nuclei; fusion splits heavy ones
Fission splits heavy nuclei and runs power plants; fusion joins light nuclei and powers the sun
Fusion is used in power plants; fission powers the sun
review.why: Fission splits uranium in reactors; fusion joins hydrogen into helium in stars.

review.q: Why can carbon-14 date a 3,000-year-old wooden tool but not a 300-million-year-old Illinois coal seam?
choices: Coal has no carbon in it
After thousands of half-lives, no measurable carbon-14 remains in the coal
review.why: Carbon-14's 5,730-year half-life makes it useless beyond about 50,000 years.
